claims.text: The base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric effect under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
The base alloy has poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack.
Adding approximately 3–5 wt% of a ductile, low-melting metallic component during melting and solidification will form an in situ binder phase.
A compositionally compatible FeCo-based eutectic can serve as the proposed low-melting metallic component.
The in situ binder phase will be distributed at grain boundaries and along microcracks.
The binder phase will bridge microcracks and impede crack propagation.
The ductile binder will absorb strain energy and blunt crack tips.
The caloric response is produced by a martensitic or analogous phase transformation.
The binder can reinforce the microstructure without interfering with the caloric phase transformation.
In situ formation will create coherent interfaces that preserve transformation kinetics.
The modified composite should have greater mechanical integrity than the pristine alloy.
The modified composite should attain a compressive strength approaching or exceeding 150 MPa.
The modified composite should retain a caloric-effect magnitude similar to that of the pristine alloy.
The modified composite should retain reversible caloric behavior during cyclic applied-field and pressure operation.
The intervention is expected to remain effective near the phase-transition temperature under applied magnetic fields, pressure fields, and cyclic mechanical loading.
Keeping the binder fraction sufficiently low will prevent excessive dilution of the calorically active phase.
A controlled comparison of binder-modified and unmodified samples under identical field, pressure, thermal, and mechanical cycling can test the hypothesis.
Failure to improve mechanical integrity or any measurable degradation of caloric response would falsify the hypothesis.
